articleGroups.label: der — masculine
articleGroups.mnemonic: Male beings, days, months, seasons, and compass points are almost always der.

rules.tip: Endings -ling, -ismus, -or, and -er (for people or jobs) are almost always masculine.
Days, months, seasons, compass points, male humans and animals, car brands, and alcoholic drinks are usually masculine. Das Bier is the classic exception for drinks.

articleGroups.label: die — feminine
articleGroups.mnemonic: Ends in -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tät, or -ion? Bet on die — and so does most plain -e.

rules.tip: Endings -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tät, -ion, -ik, and -ei are feminine. About 90% of non-compound nouns ending in -e are feminine too.
Female humans and animals, cardinal numbers, names of trees and flowers, ships, and aircraft are usually feminine.

articleGroups.label: das — neuter
articleGroups.mnemonic: -chen and -lein are always das, no exceptions — the single safest rule in German gender.

rules.tip: Diminutives ending in -chen and -lein are always neuter. So are many nouns ending in -tum, -ment, and -um, plus verbs used as nouns.
Colours used as nouns, chemical elements, metals, letters of the alphabet, and most continents, countries, and cities are neuter when used with an article.

strategies.title: Learn the article with the noun
strategies.tip: Treat the article and noun as one vocabulary item: learn der Tisch, not just Tisch. Colour-code your notes or flashcards to match this page: blue for der, pink for die, amber for das.

strategies.title: In compounds, only the last word counts
strategies.tip: In a compound noun, the final element alone determines the gender of the whole word — ignore everything before it.
examples: die Hand + das Tuch = das Handtuch
die Fahrt + die Karte = die Fahrkarte
